Introduction: The pericardium is a fibroserous sac which encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels.
Position: Posterior to sternum and 2<sup>nd</sup> to 6<sup>th</sup> costal cartilages.
Anterior to T5 and T8 vertebrae.
Functions: Prevents over-expansion of heart when blood volume increases.
Serves as lubricated container in which heart can contract and relax smoothly.
Acts as a shock absorber with the help of the fluid filled in pericardial cavity.

Fibrous pericardium: Fibrous pericardium is the outer layer of pericardium.
It is a sac made of tough connective tissue.
It is cone shaped bag with the apex directed above.
It defines the boundaries of the middle mediastinum.
It is pierced by following blood vessels

Fibrous pericardium.Superiorly: Continuous with adventitia of the great vessels and also pre-tracheal fascia.
Fibrous pericardium.Inferiorly: Attached to central tendon of diaphragm and a small muscular part of its left side. (Septum transversum)
Fibrous pericardium.Anteriorly: Attached to posterior surface of sternum by superior and inferior sternopericardial ligaments. (These ligaments help to retain the heart in its position in cavity.)
Fibrous pericardium.Laterally: Phrenic nerve with its accompanying pericardio-phrenic vessels passes through the fibrous pericardium.

Fibrous pericardium: Below the left 4<sup>th</sup> costal cartilage, pericardium comes in direct contact with the left half of lower area of the body of sternum due to cardiac notch.
This is important site for Paracentesis (Aspiration of pericardial fluid).

__p: The parietal and visceral layers of serous pericardium are continuous at the roots of the great vessels.
The reflections of serous pericardium occurs in two locations.
One surrounding the arteries (the aorta and the pulmonary trunk).
The second is surrounding the veins (the SVC, IVC and Pulmonary veins).
Parietal pericardium: Lines the inner surface of pericardium.
Pericardial cavity: The narrow space between the parietal and visceral layer of serous pericardium is called Pericardial cavity.

__p: It adheres to the heart and forms its outer covering.

data: It is closely applied to heart except at the grooves of heart where it is separated from heart by blood vessels.
It is reflected at the root of blood vessels to become continuous as visceral pericardium.
It develops from Somatopleuric layer of mesoderm.
It develops from Splanchnopleuric layer of mesoderm.

Contents: Heart with cardiac vessels and nerves
Lower half of the superior vena cava
Terminal part of the inferior vena cava
The terminal parts of the pulmonary veins

Blood supply.Venous drainage: Tributaries of the azygous system and internal thoracic veins.

__p: The transverse sinus is a horizontal gap betweent the arterial and venous ends of the heart tube.
Arterial end encloses the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
Venous end encloses the venae cavae and pulmonary veins.
It develops from degeneration of the central part of Dorsal mesocardium.

Introduction.Definition: The passage between the two, arterial tube and venous tube of epicardium is called Transverse sinus of pericardium

Transverse sinus of pericardium.Development: Developed from Central part of dorsal mesocardium

__p: The oblique sinus is a narrow gap behind the left atrium of heart.
The oblique sinus is also called as 'Cul-de-sac'.
It is developed due to rearrangement of veins at the venous end.

Superior: Reflection of visceral pericardium along upper margin of left atrium.

Oblique sinus.Clinical significance: Permits pulsations of the left atrium to take place freely.

Pericardial effusion/ Cardiac tamponade: Collection of fluid in the pericardial cavity is referred to as pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade.
The fluid compresses the heart and restricts venous filling durind diastole thus reducing the reducing cardiac output.

Pericardial effusion can be drained by puncturing the left fifth or sixth intercostal space just lateral to the sternum, or in the angle between the xiphoid process and left costal margin, with the needle directed upwards, backwards and to the left.
data.Ortner's syndrome: In mitral stenosis, left atrium enlarges and compresses the oesophagus causing Dysphagia.
Pericarditis: Inflammation of pericardium is called as Pericarditis.
It is often confused with MI where both shows Clavicular referred pain.
There is Pericardial Rub sound in paricarditis which is not shown in MI.
